reading.body:
CyrusOne Sterling publishes 24 MW of IT capacity in a 154,230 square foot facility, placing it in the middle tier of Virginia's disclosed data centers and accounting for 1.5% of the state's announced 1,603 MW.

At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, this translates to roughly 600 racks. The facility ranks 17th among Virginia's 25 data centers with public power figures. This ranking reflects a common pattern: Virginia hosts 330 mapped facilities but discloses capacity for fewer than one in ten. Sterling's apparent middle position may be misleading because the full distribution remains hidden.

Whether Sterling matters to AI scaling depends entirely on undisclosed specifications. The operator has not published whether the campus accepts high-density compute, whether power infrastructure can scale beyond 24 MW, or how much grid headroom exists in Northern Virginia to support expansion. Certifications are absent from the record. These gaps matter because AI workload suitability is determined by density, headroom, and upgrade capacity—not by raw megawatt count alone.
